t.7.42.1: There, all around the king as he sat, attended skilled jesters, adept in stories of many kinds, who provoked laughter.
t.7.42.3: These men, delighted, used to tell many kinds of stories, filled with jest, in the presence of the great-souled Rāghava.
t.7.42.2: Vijaya and Madhumatta, Kāśyapa, Piṅgala, Kuśa, Surāji, Kāliya, Bhadra and Dantavakra, together with Māgadha.
t.7.42.4: Then, in the course of a certain conversation, Rāghava spoke: "What stories, good friend, are current in the city and in the countryside?"
t.7.42.5: What things do the people of the city and the countryside say concerning me? And what do they say about Sītā, about Bharata, and indeed about Lakṣmaṇa?
t.7.42.6: What, then, do they say concerning Śatrughna and my mother Kaikeyī? For kings, in a new reign, do become the subject of people's talk.
t.7.42.7: When Rāma had spoken thus, Bhadra, with palms joined in reverence, said: "O King, good and well-established talk prevails among the city-dwellers."
t.7.42.8: But this victory, gentle one, founded on the slaying of Daśagrīva, is spoken of most of all by the citizens in your own city, O bull among men.
t.7.42.9: Thus addressed by Bhadra, Rāghava spoke these words: "Tell me everything exactly as it is, leaving nothing out."
t.7.42.10: Having now heard the words, good and bad, that the city-dwellers have spoken, I would do what is good and would not do what is bad.
t.7.42.11: Speak to me with confidence, without fear and free from anxiety, and tell me what the townsfolk say and what people in the countryside say as well.
t.7.42.12: Thus addressed by Rāghava, Bhadra, with joined palms and fully composed, replied to the mighty-armed one in very pleasing words.
t.7.42.13: Listen, O king, to how the citizens speak of what is good and what is bad, at the crossroads, in the markets and streets, and in the forests and groves.
t.7.42.14: Rāma accomplished a difficult feat, the building of a bridge across the ocean, a thing never done before by any of the ancients, not even by the gods together with the Dānavas.
t.7.42.15: And the unassailable Rāvaṇa has been slain together with his army and mounts, and the monkeys and the bears, together with the Rākṣasas, have been brought under your control.
t.7.42.16: Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle and recovered Sītā, Rāghava put his indignation behind him and brought her back again to his own home.
t.7.42.17: What kind of joy born of union with Sītā can there be in his heart, when she was once carried off by force by Rāvaṇa, who had lifted her onto his lap?
t.7.42.19: With our own wives, too, such conduct will have to be tolerated, for as the king acts, so the people follow him.
t.7.42.18: Moreover, she was carried off to Laṅkā, went into the Aśoka grove, and fell into the power of the rākṣasas; how is it that Rāma does not despise her?
t.7.42.20: Thus, O king, the city-dwellers speak words of many kinds, in all the cities and in the countryside as well.
t.7.42.21: Having heard these words of his, Rāghava, as one deeply distressed, said to all his friends: "How is this to be made known?"
t.7.42.22: But all of them, having saluted him with their heads to the ground and bowed low, replied to the dejected Rāghava: "It is just so; of this there is no doubt."
t.7.42.23: Having heard the words spoken by them all, Kākutstha, the scorcher of foes, then dismissed them all.
